openers.business-and-nature: Firms make most of the goods people buy, and most of the harm that comes with them. This chapter asks what a business owes to nature and to the people around it. Some answers are voluntary, like corporate social responsibility, where companies run their main business so its overall effect on society is positive. Others are tools and rules: management systems, audits, emissions standards and an EU list of activities that count as sustainable. Buyers push too, choosing what to buy and what to boycott by how products affect people, animals and the environment.

nature-gov-059.title: Making money without wrecking the world around you
nature-gov-059.text: Before World War 1, start-ups were already selling organic food and wind and solar energy. The business historian Geoffrey Jones traces green business back to them. Sustainable business means running a firm so that it makes money while keeping its harm to the environment, local communities and society as small as possible. Such firms aim at the {{ref:nature-acct-114}}: profit, people and planet, weighed together in every decision. The modern idea grew out of late-20th-century debates on {{ref:nature-eecon-209}}. The 1987 report {{ref:nature-hist-004}} shaped how private firms thought about managing the environment. A central aim is to cut the harm from making and using goods. Firms measure their carbon footprints, cut waste and redesign products to last longer. A green business offers products that cut demand for harmful ones, keeps its finances sound, respects human rights and supports inclusion of local and global communities. Sometimes tweaks are not enough. If a firm's whole model is unsustainable, becoming sustainable can mean rebuilding it, for example moving from selling cars to offering car sharing. In practice, firms often meet only the lowest standards. Real sustainability, its advocates say, needs a purpose that goes beyond simply obeying the law.

nature-gov-079.title: Nature-positive: halt the loss by 2030, recover by 2050
nature-gov-079.text: Over 90 world leaders signed the Leaders' Pledge for Nature, and the G7 committed to the goal at its 2021 summit. Nature-positive is a goal to halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030 and to achieve its full recovery by 2050. Progress is measured against a baseline of biodiversity in 2020. It was proposed as a single global goal for nature, to sit beside climate and development goals, aiming at an 'Equitable, Nature-Positive, Carbon Neutral world'. It matches the 2030 mission and 2050 vision of the {{ref:nature-gov-024}}, though that framework does not name it. What is new is its reach. Unlike earlier approaches, it covers a company's whole value chain, not just its direct impacts. It also aims for absolute gains, not merely doing less harm than before. The idea is contested. Critics call it vague and open to greenwashing, and warn of the 'financialization of nature', turning nature into something traded for money. Its 'net' approach is criticised for implying continued loss and for assuming that like-for-like compensation is possible. Supporters reply that business must be part of the solution. To keep the goal honest, the researcher Milner-Gulland proposed it needs a measured baseline, a timeframe, a target, clear actions, regular monitoring and disclosure.

nature-gov-100.title: The environmental management system: a firm's green rulebook
nature-gov-100.text: In March 1996 the ISO 14000 family of standards was first developed. Its member ISO 14001 is now the most widely used standard for an environmental management system, or EMS. An EMS is a set of policies, procedures and processes a firm uses to train staff and to monitor, summarize and report its environmental performance. Its goals are to obey legal standards more fully and to reduce waste, then to go beyond compliance. It helps an organization identify and control its impacts and set and track objectives. The system runs on a Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle, constantly reviewed and revised. Factories, service industries and government agencies can all use it. Independent bodies usually certify that a system conforms to ISO 14001. A good EMS also nudges contractors and suppliers to set up their own.

nature-gov-099.title: The environmental audit: checking a firm against the rules
nature-gov-099.text: Environmental audits do for environmental performance what financial audits do for accounts. An audit finds gaps in an organization's compliance with environmental rules and in its {{ref:nature-gov-100}}, then sets out corrective actions. There are two main types. Compliance audits check a site against the laws, regulations, permits and local codes that apply to it. Management system audits test the system itself. A multimedia audit covers all media, such as air, water and waste; a programmatic audit covers chosen areas, such as air alone. Certification to ISO 14001 does not by itself prove a firm obeys the law, though the standard requires firms to evaluate their compliance. Auditors work from a checklist called a protocol, and no standard protocol exists. Professionals still disagree whether detailed, prescriptive protocols beat flexible ones that rely on auditor expertise. Satellite imagery and digital mapping systems are an emerging audit tool.

nature-gov-096.title: The EU taxonomy: an official list of green activities
nature-gov-096.text: Early estimates put the average 'green asset ratio' of EU banks at just 2.23%. That ratio, which banks must disclose, comes from the EU taxonomy for sustainable activities. The taxonomy is a European Union classification system that defines which economic activities count as environmentally sustainable. It came into force in July 2020 as part of the {{ref:nature-gov-135}}, which aims for a carbon neutral economy by 2050. Its purpose is to prevent greenwashing, the practice of making things look greener than they are, and to help investors make informed sustainable choices. It covers six environmental objectives. They are climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, circular economy, pollution prevention, water and marine resources, and biodiversity and ecosystems. A Technical Expert Group set up in 2018 developed the technical screening criteria that judge whether an activity qualifies. The Environmental Delegated Act, published on 21 November 2023, set criteria for the remaining objectives, including protecting and restoring biodiversity and ecosystems. The taxonomy is spreading into other rules too. An EU green bond standard under development would require issuers to fund only activities aligned with it.

nature-gov-066.title: Design for the environment: cutting harm at the drawing board
nature-gov-066.text: Design for the environment cuts a product's or service's harm to health and the environment, counting impacts across its whole life. It has four parts: cleaner processing and manufacturing, greener packaging, design for disposal or reuse, and energy efficiency. Designers use {{ref:nature-acct-050}} to compare options and pick the least harmful. Claimed benefits are cost savings, lower risk, new markets and meeting regulations. Leaders of {{ref:nature-gov-059}} treat it as part of their work, along with counting life-cycle costs.

nature-gov-062.title: Corporate sustainability strategies: profit from going green
nature-gov-062.text: A 2023 Swiss survey of 514 small and medium firms found 89% had never produced a sustainability report. Corporate sustainability strategies are plans to win new revenue from sustainability while guarding against rising energy, regulation and resource costs and shifting customer views. Common strategies are innovation, collaboration, process improvement, reporting and greening the supply chain. The Sustainability Balanced Scorecard measures performance by balancing financial and non-financial, short- and long-term goals.

nature-gov-109.title: The Greenhouse Gas Protocol: counting a firm's emissions
nature-gov-109.text: Most of a company's emissions happen somewhere else. The Greenhouse Gas Protocol, the most common set of standards for measuring and tracking greenhouse gas emissions, makes that visible. The {{ref:nature-hist-032}} developed it with companies and published its first version in September 2001. It sorts an organization's emissions into Scope 1, 2 and 3. Scope 3 covers all other indirect emissions from its activities. For most businesses the great majority are Scope 3, coming from the wider supply chain rather than the site or purchased energy. Scope 3 was estimated at 75% of all emissions reported to the Carbon Disclosure Project, though it varies widely by sector. It is also hard to report accurately. In 2022 about 30% of US companies reported it, and double counting is a worry. The Science Based Targets initiative and the {{ref:nature-gov-107}} both cite the protocol, and the ISO 14064 standard is based on it.

nature-gov-068.title: Stakeholder theory: who a company answers to
nature-gov-068.text: In 1968 Eric Rhenman coined the English word stakeholder in his book Industrial Democracy and Industrial Management. R. Edward Freeman later built it into a theory. Stakeholder theory holds that a firm answers not only to its shareholders, its owners, but to every group with a relationship to it: workers, customers, suppliers and communities. The idea runs through responsible business. A review of 14,523 articles found the stakeholder view to be the most common dimension of {{ref:nature-gov-067}}. Satisfying stakeholders beyond shareholders is one reason firms take that path. The EU itself defines such responsibility as a firm being accountable for its impact on all relevant stakeholders. Critics say the stakeholder view ignores how complex the networks in partnerships between business, government and charities are.

nature-gov-067.title: Corporate social responsibility: business beyond profit
nature-gov-067.text: In 1953 Howard Bowen published Social Responsibilities of the Businessman. He argued that business leaders' duties go beyond making profit, and the book is widely seen as the founding work of corporate social responsibility, or CSR. CSR means companies running their main business responsibly and sustainably, so their overall effect on society is positive. It is a form of private self-regulation that aims to help social and environmental goals by reducing harm, such as cutting a firm's carbon footprint. Since the 1960s it has gone by many names: {{ref:nature-gov-092}}, sustainable business, corporate citizenship, responsible business. There is little agreement on a definition. A business person may see it as strategy, an activist at a campaign group as greenwash, and a government official as voluntary regulation. Firms take it up for strategic, ethical or instrumental reasons. For companies listed on a stock market it often takes the form of ESG practices and reports, covering environmental, social and governance issues. Its scope has widened from a firm's own conduct to its suppliers, how its products are used and how they are thrown away. It has also been shifting from voluntary choices toward mandatory schemes at regional, national and international levels. Whether it works is contested. Supporters say it raises long-term profits; critics say it distracts from a firm's economic role or is mere window-dressing.

nature-gov-102.title: Sustainability reporting: telling outsiders how a firm behaves
nature-gov-102.text: Enron's collapse and the 2008 financial crisis helped drive a boom in a new kind of company report. Sustainability reporting is the disclosure, voluntary or required, of a company's non-financial performance to people outside it. It covers environmental, social, economic and governance issues, grouped under the acronym ESG. It also goes by ESG reporting, non-financial reporting, CSR reporting and social reporting. It grew from environmental reporting, popular in the 1970s, and has expanded greatly over the last twenty years, spurred by awareness of the ecological crisis. It rests on the stakeholder model of {{ref:nature-gov-068}}. The Global Reporting Initiative standards are the most widely used benchmark worldwide. Critics say competing frameworks make reports hard to compare. Some firms hide negative or overstate positive environmental data, a practice linked to greenwashing.

nature-gov-077.title: Ethical consumerism: voting with your wallet
nature-gov-077.text: Every purchase is a small vote. Ethical consumerism means choosing what to buy, and what to boycott, by how products affect people, animals and the environment. It is a form of consumer activism based on this 'dollar voting'. Its rise over the last two decades is linked to the rise of {{ref:nature-gov-067}}. Company ratings first made for shoppers are now common in business sustainability ratings, and ESG ratings reach stock traders' screens. More consumers demand sustainable goods, especially when they think firms neglect the environment. Two things hold it back: routine buying that leaves no room for reflection, and competing moral demands in daily life.
